articles.title: In 1985, Charleston Museum received over 700 acres on James Island from the Dill family; 41 years later, it is putting over $15 million in easement value towards permanently blocking development
articles.summary: Charleston’s Dill Sanctuary on James Island is moving towards permanent protection after decades under the care of the Charleston Museum.
articles.body: Charleston’s Dill Sanctuary on James Island is moving towards permanent protection after decades under the care of the Charleston Museum. In April 2026, Charleston County Council approved a $3 million Greenbelt funding contribution towards a conservation easement covering more than 700 acres along the Stono River. The museum is contributing more than $15 million in easement value, with state and federal grants expected to cover the remaining cost. The decision marks a significant step towards safeguarding the property’s wildlife, historical landmarks and green landscape for future generations.Dill Sanctuary conservation deal will permanently protect James IslandThe latest decision follows a conservation effort that gained momentum in late 2025. According to Live5News, the Charleston Museum and the Lowcountry Land Trust had been working towards placing the property under a conservation easement to prevent future development while allowing the museum to continue managing the land.Reportedly, on April 28, 2026, Charleston County Council voted 5-4 in favour of contributing $3 million through its Greenbelt programme. The funding will help secure an easement valued at more than $20 million, with the museum's contribution accounting for more than $15 million in value. A conservation easement places legally binding restrictions on how land can be used.The Dill family's legacy dates back to 1985The sanctuary's future is closely tied to the Dill family's decision to leave the property to the Charleston Museum. In 1985, Pauline Dill, the last surviving Dill sister, bequeathed the land to the institution. The museum has managed it as a wildlife refuge ever since.However, the arrangement included legal complications. Live5News reported that a dispute over the will and a subsequent lawsuit resulted in restrictions requiring the museum to maintain the property as a wildlife refuge for 35 years. Those restrictions have since expired, creating a need for a more lasting arrangement.Museum director Carl Borick told Live5News that the current board and staff were committed to protecting the land but could not guarantee what future leadership might decide. The conservation easement offers a way to make that commitment legally binding, regardless of changes in management.Why does the sanctuary matter beyond its natural beautyThe 724-acre property is more than an expanse of undeveloped land. Its landscape carries evidence of thousands of years of human history, alongside habitats that support native wildlife.Live5News reported that archaeological evidence points to Native American activity in the area dating back approximately 8,000 years. The sanctuary also contains 4 Civil War batteries and two African American cemeteries associated with enslaved people.The Charleston City Paper also highlighted the property's history of colonial and antebellum plantations, its earthen Confederate fortifications and its importance as a habitat for wading birds.Among its natural features is a 6-acre wildlife pond with 3 nesting islands. The pond is considered an important rookery for threatened or endangered wood storks. The property also contains extensive live oak canopy, providing a valuable stretch of green space along the Stono River.Funding balances preservation with future growthLive5News explained that Charleston City Council had already approved a resolution supporting the Lowcountry Land Trust's application for the funding. The application involved partners including the South Carolina Conservation Bank and the National Coastal Wetland Conservation Grant Program.According to Live5News, state and federal grants will cover the remainder of the easement's value. This approach allows the land to be protected without requiring the county to fund the entire amount.The preservation effort also has practical implications for the surrounding community. City officials have argued that retaining open land can reduce the need for additional roads and other infrastructure associated with new development. Protecting the Stono River frontage and the area's existing landscape will also help maintain the character of James Island.The next chapter focuses on stewardship and public accessPermanent protection does not mean the sanctuary will become a conventional public park. The Charleston City Paper reported that the property is not open for daily visits, although the museum has offered school visits, summer camps, group tours by reservation, an annual oyster roast and other special events.The museum has also identified opportunities to improve ecological land management, including controlling invasive species and expanding educational programming. Reportedly, the city would have the right of first refusal if the museum ever decided to sell the property, adding another layer to the proposed long-term safeguards.You use AI every day. articles.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
articles.summary: Kashim Chowdhury is accused of fraudulently juggling multiple government jobs while working from home.
articles.body:
A civil servant is accused of earning almost £350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

articles.title: US ends auto-extension of work permits; international students not impacted
articles.summary: The Trump administration has finalised a rule ending automatic extensions of employment authorisation documents (EADs) for eligible foreign nationals
articles.body: The Trump administration has finalised a rule ending automatic extensions of employment authorisation documents (EADs) for eligible foreign nationals awaiting renewal of their work permits. For the Indian diaspora, the move could adversely impact over a lakh Indian spouses, largely women, of H-1B visa holders caught in decades-long green card backlogs.Last month, the administration had also signalled a longer-term plan to remove H-4 dependent spouses of H-1B workers from the categories eligible for employment authorisation altogether.The rule finalised by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) adopts, without change, an interim rule issued in October 2025 that ended automatic extensions for certain EAD renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025.Under the rule, filing a timely renewal application will no longer, by itself, allow eligible applicants to continue working beyond the expiry of their existing work permits while their applications are pending. The administration has said the measure is intended to strengthen vetting and screening before employment authorisation is renewed.The earlier framework, introduced in 2016, allowed eligible applicants to continue working for up to 180 days beyond the expiry of their EADs while renewal applications were processed. In 2022, the extension period was temporarily increased to 540 days and, from January 2025, made permanent to minimise employment disruptions caused by processing delays. The October 2025 interim rule withdrew this protection; the latest action codifies that change.The H-4 EAD provision itself was introduced in 2015, during the Obama administration, partly to address the difficulties faced by families (such as those from India) caught in lengthy employment-based green card backlogs. Under the provision, certain H-4 spouses could apply for work authorisation if their H-1B spouses were on the path to permanent residence or had obtained an extension beyond the normal six-year H-1B limit.A key challenge is that H-4 spouses can apply to renew their EADs only within 180 days of the expiry of their existing work permits. Since an H-4 spouse’s status extension must be filed alongside the H-1B worker’s extension, any delay by the employer in filing the H-1B petition can further narrow the window available for the dependent spouse’s renewal. With automatic extensions no longer available to those covered by the rule, applicants fear they could be forced to stop working while awaiting renewal of their EADs. Immigration attorneys have repeatedly flagged lengthy processing backlogs as a major concern.As of June 30, 2026, US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) reported more than 4.32 lakh pending EAD renewal applications (including those filed by H-4 visa holders) that had been awaiting a decision for at least six months. Of these, 91,000 had been pending for over 18 months.The policy has also faced legal challenges. As reported by TOI earlier, in an order dated September 10, 2026, a US district court in the Central District of California granted a preliminary injunction in favour of seven plaintiffs who challenged the rule. The court held that DHS had failed to follow the procedure required under the Administrative Procedure Act when introducing it. The relief, however, was limited to the seven plaintiffs and did not apply nationwide.Spouses of L-1 visa holders, who are in the US on intra-company transfers, are not affected by this change, as eligible L-2 spouses do not require an EAD to work.Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm, pointed out that F-1 students applying for a STEM extension of employment authorisation are also not affected by the elimination of the maximum 540-day automatic extension. They continue to receive a 180-day automatic extension upon timely filing of their STEM EAD application under a separate regulatory provision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1966, a New York art teacher paid under $100 for a thrift-store painting and kept it for nearly 60 years; after her son investigated its faded signature, experts identified it as an F.C.B. Cadell work that sold for £189,200
articles.summary: A painting bought for less than $100 at a thrift store in White Plains, New York, in 1966 has been sold for £189,200 at auction after experts identified
articles.body: A painting bought for less than $100 at a thrift store in White Plains, New York, in 1966 has been sold for £189,200 at auction after experts identified it as a work by Scottish artist Francis Campbell Boileau Cadell. According to Edinburgh auction house Lyon & Turnbull, the painting, titled 'Interior: The Lady in Black', remained in art teacher Helene Plotkin’s home for nearly six decades before her son’s investigation helped uncover its identity. The final price, including the buyer’s premium, was reported by the auction house and art-market publication Artnet News.Plotkin, who had an academic background in art history and studio practice, was drawn to the painting’s composition and use of colour when she encountered it while shopping in 1966. The work depicted an elegantly dressed woman seated in a red chair against a richly decorated interior. However, its signature was difficult to read, and its label identified it as 'Portrait of Miss Don Wauchope'. Unaware of its true provenance, Plotkin bought the picture and displayed it in her living room for years.The painting stayed with the family through decades of ordinary domestic life. Its significance came to light only after Plotkin’s son, Barry, began researching it in 2025, according to Artnet News. He used Google’s artificial intelligence assistant Gemini to examine a photograph of the work. The tool helped him decipher the signature and suggested that he investigate a label on the back of the canvas.That clue led the family to historical auction records. The painting had been sold at Christie’s in London on March 18, 1966, for £21, under the incorrect title 'Portrait of Miss Don Wauchope'. The record established an earlier point in the artwork’s history, although it remains unclear how the painting moved from the auction market to a thrift store in New York within months.The family then approached Lyon & Turnbull, whose specialists assessed the painting and confirmed its attribution to Cadell. The identification also corrected the name of the woman shown in the work: she was May Easter, one of the artist’s models, rather than Bethia Hamilton Don Wauchope. The auction house consequently gave the painting its present title, 'Interior: The Lady in Black'.A Scottish Colourist’s richly detailed interiorCadell (1883–1937) was one of the Scottish Colourists, a group of four painters associated with bold colour and modern approaches to composition. The group also included Samuel John Peploe, John Duncan Fergusson and George Leslie Hunter. Cadell was particularly known for paintings of Edinburgh interiors, portraits and still lifes.According to Lyon & Turnbull’s specialist analysis, 'Interior: The Lady in Black' was created during the 1920s, at the height of Cadell’s career. It depicts his north-facing studio at 6 Ainslie Place in Edinburgh’s Georgian New Town, with a view towards Fife. The artist bought the property in 1920, and its stylishly decorated rooms became recurring subjects in his work.The painting brings together several features associated with Cadell’s interiors: lilac walls, a polished black floor, mirrors, an ornate Louis XV-style armchair and a blue-and-white coffee set. A closed black fan tied with ribbon rests on a white tablecloth. Easter sits at the centre of the composition, wearing black clothing accented by a pink rose at her neckline. Her red hair and golden headwear add contrasting colour to the scene.The vivid red chair is another defining element. Lyon & Turnbull notes that Cadell used similar chairs as striking focal points in other works, and that fellow Scottish Colourist Peploe also incorporated the motif into some of his paintings. Cadell’s brushwork shifts between clear detail and simplified forms, using areas of bright colour to guide the viewer’s eye through the room.From a thrift-store find to a five-figure auction resultLyon & Turnbull included the painting in its Scottish Paintings & Sculpture auction in Edinburgh on June 4, 2026. It sold for £189,200, including the buyer’s premium, within its pre-sale estimate of £150,000 to £200,000. Artnet News reported the price as approximately $254,000.The sale represents a striking change in the painting’s fortunes. In 1966, Christie’s sold it for £21; six decades later, it fetched nearly £190,000. However, the story is not simply one of an unexpectedly valuable second-hand purchase. The discovery depended on the combination of historical records, technology and specialist art expertise.AI helped the family identify a potentially significant signature, but the attribution was confirmed by auction-house specialists rather than by the tool alone. The painting’s earlier auction history also helped establish its provenance, while the revised identification of Easter clarified the subject.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Wisconsin demolition expert spent years turning salvaged industrial machinery into the 300-ton Forevertron; the 50-foot-high, 120-foot-wide scrap-metal creation became the centrepiece of a roadside sculpture park
articles.summary: Somewhere in rural Wisconsin, a Victorian inventor is preparing for his final journey into space.
articles.body: Somewhere in rural Wisconsin, a Victorian inventor is preparing for his final journey into space. His spacecraft is unlike anything NASA would recognise, assembled from rusting industrial machinery, electrical equipment and discarded metal. Towering over a roadside sculpture park, this extraordinary creation is the work of a demolition expert whose imagination transformed scrap into something that belongs somewhere between science fiction and a fever dream.Known as the Forevertron, the colossal sculpture is the centrepiece of Dr. Evermor’s Art Park in Sumpter, Wisconsin. Built by the late Tom Every, it reflects a wonderfully eccentric vision of what happens when industrial salvage meets an imagination that refuses to be ordinary, states an online report by Milwaukee Uncut.A demolition expert with an inventor’s imaginationEvery, who lived from 1938 to 2020, spent decades working in demolition and collecting antique machinery. Rather than viewing discarded equipment as useless remnants of an industrial past, he saw the potential for something far more ambitious. During the 1980s, he began assembling these finds into elaborate sculptures, creating an entire fictional world around his alter ego, Dr. Evermor. The character was imagined as a Victorian-era inventor whose extraordinary engineering experiments eventually led to the creation of a machine capable of sending him into the heavens.The result was a sculpture park that feels less like a conventional art installation and more like the abandoned workshop of a mad scientist. Located along Highway 12 in Sauk County, the attraction is filled with fantastical metal creatures, enormous mechanical structures and curious assemblages that reward a closer look, adds the online report.Inside the 300-ton ForevertronAccording to Milwaukee Uncut, the Forevertron is difficult to miss. Standing 50 feet tall and stretching 120 feet across, the sculpture weighs approximately 300 tons and is regarded as the world's largest scrap-metal sculpture. Its construction is as remarkable as its scale. The installation incorporates two Thomas Edison dynamos dating to the 1880s, lightning rods, high-voltage equipment salvaged from 1920s power plants and metal recovered from the nearby Badger Army Ammunition Plant. Among its unusual components is a decontamination chamber associated with the Apollo 11 spacecraft.Every brought these disparate pieces together to create a machine that appears ready to generate an impossible amount of electricity. Within the mythology surrounding the artwork, the Forevertron uses a magnetic lightning force beam to propel Dr. Evermor into space. Despite its immense size, the sculpture was designed in sections connected by bolts and pins, allowing it to be dismantled and relocated if necessary, adds the report.A park populated by metal creaturesThe Forevertron may be the main attraction, but the surrounding sculpture park offers plenty more to explore. One of its most memorable installations is the Bird Band Orchestra, a gathering of around 70 birdlike metal structures arranged as though they were performing together. Elsewhere, satellite and telescope installations sit alongside smaller, insect-like creations and fantastical mechanical forms. Rust, weathered surfaces and mismatched industrial components give the entire collection a distinctly otherworldly character.Where discarded machinery finds a second lifeFor travellers exploring Wisconsin Dells or the western reaches of Wisconsin, Dr. Evermor’s Art Park offers an unusual detour. It is a reminder that creativity does not always begin with a blank canvas or pristine materials. Sometimes, it begins with what the world has thrown away. In Every’s hands, forgotten machinery became an elaborate universe of its own, with the Forevertron standing as its monumental centrepiece.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Milwaukee UncutYou use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Four Indians injured in an October 10 attack in Saudi Arabia remain hospitalised, including four in intensive care, the ministry of external
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Four Indians injured in an October 10 attack in Saudi Arabia remain hospitalised, including four in intensive care, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said on Wednesday. The ministry condemned the recent attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure, including an assault on Aramco headquarters, and called for an immediate halt to such strikes.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said 12 people were injured in the October 10 incident. One of them later died. His last rites were performed in Riyadh, as wished by his family, with assistance from the Indian embassy. Of the 11 surviving injured people, three have been discharged, while eight remain in hospital, including four in the ICU."Embassy officials are regularly visiting them and staying in touch with their families," Jaiswal said, adding that India remained committed to ensuring the welfare of its nationals abroad.MEA condemns attacks, stands with Saudi ArabiaCondemning the latest attacks on Saudi Arabia, Jaiswal said India stood in solidarity with the country's people and government."There has been a string of attacks in Saudi Arabia, including yesterday’s attack on Aramco headquarters. We condemn all such attacks on civilian infrastructure and call for them to cease immediately. They are totally unacceptable. We stand in solidarity with the people and government of Saudi Arabia in defence of their sovereignty and hope for a return to peace and normalcy in the region," he said.Flights disrupted, embassy issues advisoriesThe attacks have also disrupted flight schedules, affecting Indian carriers and passengers travelling to and from Saudi Arabia."Flight schedules have been disrupted following attacks on airports, impacting Indian carriers, particularly flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam, Medina and Jeddah," Jaiswal said.The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia is in regular contact with the Indian community. It has issued advisories and is providing updated information to travellers and passengers stranded by the disruptions."Our embassy in Saudi Arabia is in regular touch with the Indian community and has issued advisories for their welfare. The embassy is providing updated information to travellers and those stranded," Jaiswal said.Attacks raise security concernsThe latest developments come amid a series of attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil infrastructure. Yemen's Houthi rebels sent out missles and drones striking Saudi locations and emergency facilities.The attacks have raised concerns over the security of critical infrastructure and the impact on civilian travel. articles.title: US inflation rises more than expected ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
articles.body:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.

Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have spiked following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.

Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.

In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.

Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.

Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.

At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?

While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect prices to fall further. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

articles.body: MEERUT: Punishing the guilty in accordance with the gravity of their crime is also Dharma, a Meerut court observed on Wednesday while sentencing Muskan Rastogi and her lover Sahil Shukla to death in the blue drum murder case, prosecution lawyer KK Chaubey said.District and sessions judge Arvind Kumar Mishra invoked the Mahabharata while pronouncing the sentence, drawing on the epic to explain the principle behind the punishment awarded to the two convicts, Chaubey said.The court sentenced Muskan and Sahil to death for murdering Muskan’s husband, Saurabh Rajput, a former Merchant Navy officer, and destroying evidence.It also imposed fines of Rs 50,000 each under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (murder) and Rs 20,000 each under Section 238(A) for causing the disappearance of evidence. Both appeared before the court through video conferencing.The case dates back to March 2025, when Rajput, 35, was allegedly killed by the duo.Police said his body was dismembered and the remains concealed in a blue plastic drum filled with cement. The crime came to light after a foul smell emanating from the drum led to the discovery of the remains.Rajput had returned to Meerut from London in late February 2025 and was killed on March 4. Police alleged that Muskan and Sahil drugged him before stabbing him to death. The two were arrested after returning from a trip to Himachal Pradesh.The trial involved the examination of 22 prosecution witnesses and more than 100 hearings.Rajput’s mother, Renu Devi, was present at the court when the verdict was pronounced.“My son cannot come back but I had prayed every day for the last 18 months that they should be given death sentence. articles.title: In 1991, Steve Harvey was homeless, sleeping in his car with just $35; after his Apollo breakthrough, his foundation went on to award more than $700,000 in scholarships and build mentoring programs for underserved youth
articles.summary: In 1991, Steve Harvey was living in his Ford Tempo with just $35 in his pocket.
articles.body: In 1991, Steve Harvey was living in his Ford Tempo with just $35 in his pocket. Years later, an unexpected invitation to perform on New York’s famous Showtime at the Apollo helped change his career. Today, the television host and comedian supports young people through charitable work, with his foundation awarding more than $700,000 in college scholarships. Harvey’s journey from a struggling stand-up comedian to a philanthropist reflects the work of the Steve & Marjorie Harvey Foundation. The organisation was established to support young people from underserved communities and single parents across the United States.A turning point at the Apollo TheatreBefore becoming a nationally known entertainer, Harvey spent three years living in his car while trying to build a career in comedy. He kept his belongings in two bags, used petrol station facilities to wash and relied on payphones to manage his finances. In a personal account published on his official website, SteveHarvey.com, Harvey described 1991 as a turning point in his life. "In 1991 I was sleeping in my car, I had $35 to my name," Harvey stated in a personal account published on the platform. "In 1991 I was sleeping in my car, I had $35 to my name, everything I had could fit into two bags. I started talking to God about my dreams… Fast forward, out of nowhere I get a call from the Apollo asking me to come on the show." His televised performance at Harlem's Apollo Theatre became a major step forward in his career. It led to regular hosting work on the show and later opportunities in television sitcoms, syndicated radio and major game shows. Looking back on that period, Harvey spoke about the choice people face when financial hardship makes success seem out of reach. "Everybody has a turn back a moment, it's the moment you can either go forward or give everything up," Harvey shared on his website. "There's one guarantee if you give up it will never happen. Faith is everything, God is always on time, he's never too late."Financial backing for higher educationAfter building a successful entertainment career, Harvey and his wife, Marjorie Harvey, established the Steve & Marjorie Harvey Foundation. The organisation aims to help young people from low-income backgrounds overcome educational and social barriers. According to figures published on the foundation's official website, the non-profit organisation has awarded more than $700,000 in academic scholarships over ten years. The support ranges from allowances for books to $15,000 per semester for individual students. The foundation also reported on its website that it has awarded nearly 100 scholarships to college students. The programme aims to help students continue their education without financial difficulties forcing them to stop their studies. "We have granted close to 100 scholarships to deserving youth through our Scholarship program, enabling our future leaders to continue to pursue their academic endeavors," the Steve & Marjorie Harvey Foundation stated on its website. "We believe that these scholarships will create a legacy for families and generations to come." The scholarship programme includes direct tuition support and partnerships with educational organisations. The foundation also holds annual college and career fairs, where students can meet university representatives and learn about scholarship opportunities. These efforts are intended to make higher education more accessible to students who might otherwise struggle to cover the cost of their studies.Mentoring networks for young men and womenAlongside its financial support for college students, the foundation runs programmes focused on young people's development, leadership skills and mental wellbeing. According to the organisation's published materials, its main initiatives include the Steve Harvey Mentoring Program for Young Men and Marjorie Harvey's Girls Who Rule The World. The young men's programme teaches personal responsibility, leadership and the value of positive role models. Through organised camps and follow-up activities, participants meet business leaders, educators and community mentors who can guide them as they prepare for adulthood. "This program helps young men realize their potential and envision and prepare for a robust and productive future," the foundation explained on its official about page. "SHMP aims to break the misguided traits of manhood and introduce role models who provide positive examples of manhood." The Girls Who Rule The World programme offers similar guidance to young women. Its focus includes building self-confidence, supporting academic achievement, providing career advice and introducing participants to different cultures and experiences. The foundation also runs enrichment workshops for single mothers. These sessions offer practical advice on managing money, maintaining emotional wellbeing and making parenting decisions. The aim is to help parents raise their children while dealing with difficult personal and financial circumstances. Through scholarships, mentoring camps and community programmes, the Steve & Marjorie Harvey Foundation continues to support young people and families across North America. Its work brings together educational assistance, personal guidance and practical resources for people seeking better opportunities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Mumbai restaurants to hike prices by 10-15% from next week; your idli, dosa and dal-rice meals to cost more
articles.summary: MUMBAI: For a Mumbaikar who begins the day with idli at a neighbourhood Udupi restaurant and depends on a simple dal-rice meal for lunch, eating out could
articles.body: MUMBAI: For a Mumbaikar who begins the day with idli at a neighbourhood Udupi restaurant and depends on a simple dal-rice meal for lunch, eating out could soon take a bigger bite out of the monthly budget.Restaurants across the city are likely to increase menu prices by 10% to 15% in the coming weeks, the Indian Hotel & Restaurant Association (AHAR) announced on Wednesday, citing rising cooking-gas, food, rental, labour and transportation costs.The rise will come into effect from next week, said AHAR President Vijay Shetty.The increase may look modest on an individual bill. But for office-goers who eat out daily, students living away from home, delivery-dependent professionals and families that order meals when time is short, the additional expense could accumulate over a month."On every menu the rise will be minimum Rs 10 if calculated on an average for menus such as idli, dosai and daal rice," Shetty said.AHAR has over 25000 member restaurants and bars.Online menus listed by Mumbai restaurants and food-delivery platforms provide a useful indication of the potential impact.Udupi Cafe in Powai lists idli at Rs 80, sada dosa at Rs 90 and dal khichdi at Rs 120.At Udupi 2 Mumbai's Dadar East outlet, listed prices include Rs 120 for steamed idli, Rs 130 for sada dosa and Rs 165 for masala dosa. These are published online menu prices, not a citywide average or a uniform dine-in tariff.If the proposed 10%-15% revision were applied to these prices, an Rs 80 serving of idli would cost Rs 88 to Rs 92, a Rs 90 sada dosa Rs 99 to Rs 104 and a Rs 165 masala dosa about Rs 182 to Rs 190.The actual increase will depend on whether an establishment revises its prices and by how much.What your everyday meal could costThe spread in dal-rice prices is significant.Swiggy listings show dal-rice at Rs 140 at Jyoti Refreshment in Dadar East and Rs 175 at Neo Welcome Restaurant in Ghatkopar West.These are individual outlet prices, not a representative average for Mumbai's eateries. They nevertheless show why the effect on customers will differ according to where they eat.The monthly bill: A small increase that adds upConsider an office-goer who spends ₹150 a day on breakfast and lunch. If the entire spend rises by 10%-15%, the daily outlay would increase to Rs 165 to Rs 172.50.Over 26 working days, the additional expense would be Rs 390 to Rs 585. For two working adults in a household with similar eating-out habits, the combined increase could approach Rs 780 to Rs 1,170 a month.For a student or a worker who relies on an inexpensive neighbourhood eatery, that could mean cutting back on snacks, ordering less frequently or carrying food from home more often.Why restaurants say they cannot absorb the costsAHAR president Vijay K Shetty said restaurants had absorbed rising expenses for as long as possible, but simultaneous increases in several operating costs had made this increasingly difficult.Commercial LPG and piped gas are essential to everyday kitchen operations. Restaurants must also pay for vegetables, pulses, milk, dairy products, edible oils and other groceries, besides transport and logistics to bring supplies to their premises.Commercial rentals and real-estate costs add to the pressure, particularly in Mumbai's busy business districts and high-footfall neighbourhoods. Restaurants must also meet wage bills, maintenance costs, utility expenses, equipment requirements and other operating obligations.The pressure on pulses is not limited to restaurant kitchens. A Times of India report published in October documented retail dal prices rising by Rs 20 to Rs 30 per kg across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region, following a Rs 10 to Rs 20 per kg increase in wholesale prices at Vashi APMC.The report attributed the increase to supply shortages, deficient monsoon rainfall, drought conditions, logistics costs and festive-season demand.For a restaurant buying ingredients in bulk, such movements can add to the difficulty of keeping a familiar meal affordable. The extent of the effect on any particular menu, however, depends on its ingredients, quantities, procurement arrangements and other costs.When the kitchen bill becomes a customer billThe problem has surfaced before.In April 2026, another media organisation reported that Udupi Shri Krishna in Lower Parel had raised prices by 20% amid a commercial LPG supply crunch.A vegetable sandwich that had cost Rs 70 was priced at Rs 90, while pav bhaji and uttapam also became more expensive.The report described how restaurants were struggling with fuel availability and rising ingredient and packaging costs.That earlier episode illustrates the dilemma: a restaurant cannot indefinitely absorb higher operating expenses, but every price increase risks making regular customers reconsider how often they eat there.A neighbourhood khanaval serving dal, rice, chapati and vegetables faces the same balancing act. Its customers may be workers who cannot return home for lunch.If a meal becomes more expensive, they feel the difference directly; if the owner holds prices down while costs rise, the business has less room to pay staff and maintain operations.No blanket increase across all restaurantsAHAR said the proposed revision would be implemented individually by establishments, depending on their cost structures and business models. It could affect dine-in restaurants, quick-service outlets and delivery businesses differently.“This is not a price increase undertaken for profiteering. It is a necessary adjustment to ensure that restaurants can continue to maintain the quality of food, hygiene, service and employment that our customers expect,” Shetty said.The association's announcement does not mean every restaurant has already raised prices, nor does it establish a mandatory or uniform rate. Customers should check the current menu at their regular outlets before assuming that a hike has taken effect.For Mumbai's restaurant industry, the immediate challenge is to keep businesses viable as costs rise. He was also rearing country chickens and a pet dog on the premises. According to sources, nearly 15,000 coconuts were stored in the godown. Arumugam lives elsewhere in the area.In the early hours of Wednesday, unidentified people allegedly set fire to the two thatched houses and the coconut storage shed. The flames spread rapidly, engulfing the entire premises.On receiving information, personnel from the Rasipuram fire and rescue services station rushed to the spot and extinguished the blaze.Namagiripettai police registered a case. articles.title: Explore Bhitarkanika with luxury floating this puja season
articles.summary: Luxury river cruises in Odisha’s Bhitarkanika National Park draw Puja tourists, offering solar-powered floating stays to spot mangrove wildlife safely.
articles.body: Kendrapada: Want to spend the Puja holidays with Mother nature, floating amid tranquillity, away from the hustle-bustle of the city.River cruise tourism in Bhitarkanika National Park, which is emerging as a major attraction this puja season, will offer visitors a unique opportunity to explore India's second-largest mangrove forest while enjoying the comfort of luxury floating accommodation.Cruising through a network of tidal rivers and narrow creeks surrounded by dense mangrove forests, tourists can witness the rich biodiversity of Bhitarkanika, including saltwater crocodiles, spotted deer, wild boars, fishing cats, leopard cats, water monitors and a variety of birds from a safe distance.A tourist said the journey offered an excellent way to explore the mangrove forest and observe its wildlife.Bhitarkanika National Park is gearing up for a major tourist rush during the puja season, with hotels, resorts, lodges and homestays also reporting strong bookings.Forest department, which had purchased four luxury boats in 2010, had handed over four eco-friendly catamaran boats to a private tour operator in 2024 to promote the river cruise tourism in the region.The operator subsequently renovated all four vessels, installing solar panels, air-conditioning systems and other modern amenities. Each boat can accommodate up to six tourists and is equipped with safety mechanisms. The soundless, fibre-bodied vessels are designed to offer a comfortable experience while minimising disturbance to the surrounding environment.“Besides comfort, the boats are equipped with safety features to ensure tourists remain safe while exploring the waterways of the mangrove forest, which is home to around 1,800 saltwater crocodiles,” said Sanghamitra Jena, head of operations.The boats feature two bedrooms, balconies with comfortable seating, attached bathrooms, dining areas and kitchens, making them similar to floating hotels.Although tourists are not permitted to enter the core area of the mangrove forest, the cruises allow them to view parts of the protected landscape and observe its wildlife.Demand for cruises has increased, with several overseas tourists also opting to stay overnight. For a family of six, it would cost around Rs 1.5 lakh for a two-night stay, according to the operator.The growing popularity of river cruises has also contributed to an increase in tourist accommodation around Bhitarkanika, with several hotels and buildings coming up.Assistant conservator of forests (ACF), Bhitarkanika, Gagan Bihari Mallick, said the river cruise tourism had become increasingly popular in the region.Tourists can enjoy the serene waterways of the Patasala, Brahmani and Baitarani rivers while visiting places such as Aradi, Chandabali, Kanika Island and Dharma. The cruises offer opportunities to enjoy peaceful sunsets, scenic landscapes and the tranquillity of the mangrove ecosystem.A retired officer who recently spent two nights aboard a cruise boat with his family described the experience as an opportunity to spend peaceful time amid nature.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhubaneswar | Silver Rate in Bhubaneswar | Bank Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Public Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Petrol Price in Bhubaneswar | Diesel Price in Bhubaneswar | CNG Price in Bhubaneswar | LPG Price in BhubaneswarStay updated with the latest Bhubaneswar news. articles.title: London Stock Exchange, NSE IFSC explore cross-border listings, trading
articles.summary: LSE and NSE IFSC sign MoU to explore cross-border listings and trading in equities, bonds, ETFs and derivatives linked to FTSE Russell indices.
articles.body: Ahmedabad: The London Stock Exchange (LSE) and NSE IFSC Ltd (NSEIX) signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Wednesday to explore cross-border listings, trading, and new financial products. The agreement aims to deepen capital market links between India and the UK.The exchanges will explore dual and cross-listings in equities, fixed-income securities and exchange-traded funds (ETFs). They will also examine trading in existing financial products and the development of NSEIX-linked derivatives tied to FTSE Russell indices.The proposed collaboration also covers new equity indices, cross-border trading connectivity and market data distribution.Based at GIFT City, NSEIX offers single-stock and index derivatives, currency derivatives, depository receipts and global stocks. Its primary market products include equity shares, debt securities, real estate investment trusts (REITs) and infrastructure investment trusts (InvITs).The initiative follows the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA). “The agreement aims to open up opportunities in capital market connectivity and financial services integration between the two countries,” NSEIX managing director and chief executive V Balasubramaniam said. “The proposed collaboration could enable trading in both directions. It could also improve liquidity and widen the investor base. NSEIX’s presence in the GIFT International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) ecosystem and the London Stock Exchange’s established market position could help deepen financial market links between the two countries.”Dame Julia Hoggett, chief executive of London Stock Exchange plc and head of digital and securities markets at London Stock Exchange Group, said the agreement would help connect the two markets. articles.title: Deoghar DC orders tighter surveillance around airport
articles.summary: Deoghar DC Saurabh Bhuwania orders tighter airport surveillance to curb encroachments, ensure DGCA mock drills, and improve cleanliness and passenger facilities.
articles.body: Dumka: Deoghar deputy commissioner Saurabh Kumar Bhuwania on Wednesday directed officials to intensify surveillance around Deoghar airport to prevent unauthorised construction and encroachments that could pose a risk to aircraft operations.At a review meeting, Bhuwania took stock of the proposed airport expansion, security arrangements and passenger facilities. He asked airport authorities to monitor construction activity in the vicinity and take action against structures built in violation of prescribed norms.“Any activity that poses a risk to the safe operation of aircraft will not be tolerated. Strict vigilance must be maintained against encroachments and illegal constructions around the airport,” he said.Bhuwania also directed officials to strengthen emergency preparedness through regular mock drills in accordance with Directorate General of Civil Aviation guidelines. He said the exercises were essential to improve the response of personnel during emergencies and ensure safe aircraft operations.He instructed the airport management to maintain cleanliness, improve passenger facilities and ensure close coordination with the civil administration. articles.title: The Weekly Vine, Edition 111: The Toaster Lover Theory
articles.summary: Hello and welcome to the 111th edition of the Vine.
articles.body: Hello and welcome to the 111th edition of the Vine. The number 111, as any cricket fan will know, is often associated with Lord Nelson, whose three famous naval victories are sometimes said to explain the number (won, won, won), and who became the victim of fake news that he had one eye, one arm and one leg. The number became immortalised in cricketing history thanks to umpire David Shepherd, who would hop, lift one leg off the ground or do a little jig to ward off bad luck.But the 111th edition doesn't deal with Nelson, but with another British protagonist – and Indian antagonist – Winston Churchill, a man whose provocations one ought to take seriously because he consumed bacon and whisky for breakfast. After a major Allied victory at the Second Battle of El Alamein in North Africa, Churchill announced: “Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.”The great proponent of intermittent fasting made the remark to temper British public expectations, and it has lived on in public memory as one of the most famous examples of political rhetoric. One instantly thought of Churchill when a headline in a piece published in an imperial media outlet blared: “Is This the Beginning of the End of Indian Democracy?”Now, Betteridge’s Law of Headlines states that any headline ending in a question mark can be dismissed with a firm “No”, but this was a venerable magazine, named after the only city that aliens ever consider attacking.Carrying this magazine’s tote bag instantly increases one’s standing everywhere from South Delhi to South Mumbai. After all, carrying said tote is a sign that one is well-read and well-bred, can perceive the difference between an Americano and a mocha, knows there is a special rung in hell for those who mix Coke with Scotch, and perhaps reads Proust in one’s free time.So one ploughed on, only to discover that the piece was actually a Q&A with a famous psephologist who has an excellent beard and a grim expression that he usually reserves for national television whenever his predictions go wrong or a party he dislikes wins, which sadly happens rather too often for comfort. There’s nothing new about biased media coverage from Anglosphere outlets, but what is it that lets so many ostensibly smart people, blessed to speak the language of Shakespeare, get the world’s largest democracy so wrong?The answer, as usual, lies in a strange modern-day iteration of the Orwellian concept of groupthink: The Toaster Lover Theory.The term groupthink was coined by William H Whyte Jr in a March 1952 article for Fortune magazine, inspired by George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, which, as the Vine has argued in the past, should be compulsory reading about dystopia along with Brave New World and Fahrenheit 451.Whyte was rather concerned that Americans – despite professing devotion to individualism – were increasingly surrendering their independent judgement to the collective. He labelled the herd instinct rationalised conformity, where being part of a tribe was deemed more acceptable than thinking for oneself. From an evolutionary perspective, when troglodytes had to stick together to ward off wild beasts, that made a lot of sense.Two decades later, Yale psychologist Irving Janis expanded the concept in his 1972 book Victims of Groupthink, examining how highly intelligent people could arrive at spectacularly stupid decisions because everyone was too concerned about preserving consensus to question the prevailing wisdom. One of his examples was the Bay of Pigs fiasco, when some of the finest minds in the Kennedy administration decided that sending CIA-backed Cuban exiles to overthrow Fidel Castro was an excellent idea. But Castro would not be overthrown, continuing to give seven-hour-long speeches, finally shuffling off his mortal coil at the age of 90, by which time he had even outlived most of his obit writers.Janis believed that being part of a group developed an illusion of unanimity, suppressed doubts and rationalised contrary evidence. Nobody wanted to play the Devil’s advocate in situations like this. And then came the internet, where everyone could select their own intellectual companions, block anyone who disagreed and spend every waking hour being informed that their political views weren’t just correct but morally superior.And that brings us to the modern-day version of groupthink, but this time on forums: the Toaster Lover Theory.On 7 January 2021, a day after the storming of the US Capitol, a commenter called ‘tonfreed’ on Hacker News described a problem involving a gentleman with unusual amorous intentions towards a toaster. His original terminology was considerably less family-friendly, so for the purposes of the Vine, we shall call it the Toaster Lover Theory. Since then, like a Dawkinsian meme, the idea has travelled through internet forums, including Reddit, and found its way into an earlier edition of the Vine.The premise is deliciously simple.Pre-internet, if a gentleman announced to his friends that he wanted to perform coitus on an electrical appliance, his friends would mock him, deride him, recommend therapy and remove any kitchen equipment from his vicinity. Shame was once the ultimate blocker. And then came the World Wide Web, or perhaps we ought to call it the World Wild Web.Now, a gentleman who feels proper amore for his toaster can simply go online and discover a thousand other folks who share his enthusiasm for breakfast equipment. Soon, they will have a subreddit, a Discord server, a flag and a manifesto explaining how history has surgically oppressed toaster-attracted individuals.Ergo, the eccentricity becomes a community, the community becomes an identity, and then the identity infiltrates the Democratic Party.Anyone suggesting that intercourse with kitchen equipment is not copacetic or is medically inadvisable is dismissed as a bigot, a prude or someone who secretly prefers a two-slice model. Things get so bad that normal people, fed up with being told they are bigots for pointing out that one shouldn’t perform coitus with an electrical appliance, instead vote for a reality TV star who has his own bizarre cult of toaster lovers.The internet didn’t invent human strangeness; it has always survived in the deeper recesses of the human mind, and the twain didn’t meet because two people with the same eccentricity often faced either a linguistic or a geographical barrier. But once any eccentricity acquires enough followers, someone invariably starts a podcast.There is considerable academic research explaining why this happens.Cass Sunstein, the American legal scholar, has extensively explored group polarisation, the tendency of like-minded people to adopt more extreme positions after discussing their opinions among themselves. Put ten Manchester United fans in a room to discuss Pep Guardiola, and by the end of the evening, they might conclude that he is personally responsible for everything wrong with modern football. Perhaps he is.Then there is the false consensus effect, demonstrated by psychologists Lee Ross, David Greene and Pamela House in 1977, which describes our tendency to overestimate how many people share our opinions. Ergo, our toaster enthusiast, having discovered several thousand like-minded individuals, starts believing that his affection for electrical appliances represents an ordinary human experience, conveniently ignoring the billions who have never considered breakfast preparation a form of foreplay.Another related phenomenon is the availability cascade, described by Timur Kuran and Cass R Sunstein in 1999, which states that an assertion becomes increasingly plausible simply because more people keep repeating it, and the popularity of an idea subsumes any evidence for its accuracy.Add John Suler’s 2004 research on online disinhibition, which explains why people do things online that they would never contemplate face to face, and we have the psychological foundations of the modern internet.The scale of this phenomenon is rather extraordinary.In 2017, researchers at MIT examined 126,000 cascades of true and false stories on Twitter between 2006 and 2017 – before it became the hellhole known as X – and found that falsehoods were 70% more likely to be retweeted than the truth. False stories also reached 1,500 people six times faster than the truth, showing that the old maxim about a lie travelling halfway across the world before the truth can tie its shoelaces was scientifically accurate.Add to that the massive echo-chamber problem: a 2021 study published in PNAS examined more than 100 million pieces of content across various platforms and found that people frequently clustered around like-minded opinions, becoming the literal version of what is known online as a cluster***.And if all that wasn’t bad enough, we now have algorithms that amplify these inaccuracies, including X, where, if you accidentally click on one video questioning whether the moon landings happened, you will soon be inundated with information that the pyramids were constructed by aliens and that everyone, including the Vatican, the Rothschilds and George Soros, has been conspiring for centuries to hide that truth from civilisation.For too long, mainstream Anglosphere media outlets have operated under the delusion that this peculiar affliction affects only fringe groups, whether MAGA conspiracy theorists, Flat Earthers or those in India who proudly possess degrees from WhatsApp University.But the Toaster Lover Theory applies just as readily to journalists, academics, political commentators and the intellectual classes whose collective wisdom is supposed to protect the rest of us from misinformation.Consider how many different mendacities have acquired something resembling a consensus among major Anglosphere outlets.Off the top of my head, there was the insistence that Joe Biden was sharp as a tack; that Kamala Harris was a brilliant communicator; that suggesting COVID-19 might have originated in a laboratory was preposterous and perhaps even racist; that Donald Trump was practically a Russian plant; that Hunter Biden’s laptop was just a MAGA conspiracy theory; and that Pakistani grooming gangs didn’t exist.The point isn’t simply that journalists from organisations of note fell for mendacities that backed their worldview, but how particular interpretations can harden into professional consensus where even an alternative suggestion is shouted down.The truth is that the internet’s echo chambers aren’t populated only by eccentric men living in their mother's basement who feel amour proper for a toaster, but also by those whose job is to inform us about the truth as it stands, not the gospel truth created in their heads by their worldview.So, to answer the question posed by that venerable magazine: “Is this the beginning of the end of Indian democracy?” To paraphrase Churchill, it is neither the end, nor the beginning of the end, nor even the end of the beginning.Indian democracy has survived the Emergency, assassinations, insurgencies, separatist movements, caste conflicts, religious riots and politicians whose greatest contribution to public life has been their inability to distinguish public money from personal property. The modern Indian state might have emerged in 1947, but the civilisation it governs has spent millennia accommodating contradictions that would give the average Western political commentator a nervous breakdown.And perhaps that's the ultimate lesson of the Toaster Lover Theory.The internet has allowed every eccentric to find people who share his convictions, but the truly remarkable development is how the same mechanism has conquered institutions supposedly dedicated to independent thought. The original toaster enthusiasts, at least, had the decency to confine their delusions to the kitchen. Their better-educated cousins have acquired prestigious bylines, editorial boards and the conviction that they alone can explain the world to the rest of us.And for those wondering, yes, I do have the tote bag: It hangs outside my door to collect my groceries.Also readRandom Musing: Why our AI choices are ‘Black’ George Washington or MechaHitlerThe Weekly Vine, Edition 106: The radical thing you should do instead of the ’80s AI photo challengeThe Weekly Vine, Edition 91: PM’s economy appeal, Starmer’s ‘Labour pain’, and cooking kosha mangshoWhy Indians are among the wildest bunch on the World Wide WebPostscript by Prasad Sanyal: The donkey between two haystacksJean Buridan, who taught philosophy at the University of Paris in the fourteenth century and was twice its rector, never actually wrote about a donkey, which makes him the first of many intellectuals to be remembered chiefly for something a critic made up. The animal was attached to his name later, most likely by people who wished to mock his view that the will, faced with two equal goods, must wait for the intellect to tell it which is better.The joke they built is simple enough: place a hungry ass exactly midway between two identical haystacks, and it will starve, because it has no reason to prefer the left over the right. Aristotle had floated a version of this: a man as hungry as he was thirsty, stranded between food and drink; Spinoza, centuries later, conceded that such a creature would indeed perish, and wondered whether we ought to call it a man or an ass, a question I have since heard put, in less elegant terms, at several appraisal meetings.Read more.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Musk of crippling Starlink as ties with US worsen following Trump's Russia diesel deal
articles.summary: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of restricting its Starlink satellite internet services without warning, disrupting military drone operations as
articles.body: Ukraine has accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of restricting its Starlink satellite internet services without warning, disrupting military drone operations as Russian missile strikes damaged power stations and left hundreds of thousands of people without electricity.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Moscow's latest attacks as an act of "ostentatious disrespect" towards US President Donald Trump, who had announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking energy infrastructure. Neither side had formally confirmed the reported ceasefire, and Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities continued.The developments come amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and criticised Zelenskyy. Trump, seeking to bring down fuel prices that have risen since the US launched a war against Iran, has urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and suggested that Zelenskyy should be replaced.Starlink disruptions raise concerns in KyivUkrainian military officials said SpaceX had interrupted Starlink connections on military-grade terminals moving at high speeds, making it difficult for the country to use the satellite internet system to guide drones."Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the country's south-east, said the connection had been dropping for 10 to 20 seconds when drones travelled at speeds of just 110 to 120 kmph."The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," the corps said in a statement to news agency Reuters.A source in Ukraine's Defence Ministry said the restrictions had significantly complicated logistics and some drone operations.The apparent disruption prompted criticism from Poland, which pays for Ukraine's Starlink subscriptions. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski directly challenged Musk over the issue."Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you ​playing politics with your products again?" Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."Musk did not immediately respond, while SpaceX did not immediately reply to a request for comment outside US business hours. Musk has previously called Sikorski a "small man".The reported restrictions have heightened Ukrainian concerns that Washington and its allies could reduce military support to pressure Kyiv into accepting concessions to Moscow. Sources have told Reuters and other news organisations that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence used to provide early warnings of Russian missile strikes unless Ukraine suspends attacks on Russian oil refineries.Russian strikes leavethousands without powerRussian missile attacks struck energy facilities in and around Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, during hours of bombardment.Officials said around 600,000 people were left without electricity. Zelenskyy said more than 30 power stations had been damaged, while Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed strikes on four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets.In Kyiv, rescue workers carried injured people away from the wreckage of a damaged residential building overnight as firefighters battled a large blaze. Officials reported two deaths and 21 injuries at the site.Ukrainian officials said they had received no advance warning from Western partners about the major Russian attacks for a second consecutive day. Trump, however, insisted on Tuesday that Washington was continuing to share intelligence with Kyiv.Zelenskyy accused Moscow of deliberately disregarding Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire."Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."Zelenskyy said Ukraine was prepared to observe the proposed truce and had refrained from attacking Russian refineries since Trump's announcement. However, he warned that Kyiv would not continue to hold back if Russia kept striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.The Kremlin said on Tuesday that discussions over an energy ceasefire were continuing.Ukraine said it had intercepted only four of the 39 Russian missiles launched in the latest attacks, highlighting the strain on its air defences amid shortages of weapons. The country's ability to counter fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones has been a particular concern.Why Starlink matters to Ukraine's militaryStarlink has been a critical communications system for Ukraine since SpaceX activated the service in the country in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.Its resistance to electronic jamming has made it particularly valuable for military communications, helping Ukrainian forces coordinate operations, guide long-range attack drones and operate drones that deliver supplies to frontline troops.Although Starlink does not operate inside Russia and Ukrainian drones attacking Russian oil infrastructure use other communication methods, Kyiv relies on the system to control drones over Ukrainian territory, including areas occupied by Russian forces.Any sustained disruption could therefore affect battlefield communications, drone operations and the delivery of supplies to troops.Musk is a close political ally of Trump, adding another layer of concern for Kyiv as it faces continued Russian attacks, uncertainty over Western intelligence support and growing pressure from Washington to agree to limits on its military operations.You use AI every day.
